name: William Somerville
summary: The narrator: William Somerville, born 1937, the family historian whose recorded conversation is the foundation of this archive. Son of {p:reginald-somerville|Reginald Somerville} and {p:honor-johnson|Honor Johnson}; brother of {p:juanita|Juanita}; father of {p:james-somerville|James}, {p:charles-somerville|Charles} and {p:edward-somerville|Edward}; grandfather of the interviewer, {p:interviewer|Gergely}.
bio: William Somerville, the narrator, was born in 1937 {q:516}, the son of Reginald Somerville's second marriage {q:512-514}, and describes himself as "coming up to 90" and his memory as "sadly failing" {q:50}, though the recording shows a remarkable command of six generations of detail.

{int}The recording itself never states his full name, though the interviewer seems to address him as William ("There you go, William" {q:T2:203}). His identity and immediate family (his sister Juanita; his sons James, Charles and Edward; his grandson Gergely, the interviewer, son of Charles) were confirmed by the family in 2026. Names heard in the everyday conversation fit: a James, with Holly, receives his personal-alarm alerts {q:T2:32-39}, and "Charles is back" {q:T2:120-122}.

He inherited the family's genealogical habit from his grandfather {p:bellingham-arthur-somerville|Bellingham Arthur Somerville} {q:2} and his aunt {p:cecilia-somerville|Cecilia} {q:230}, and refers to documents still in the family's keeping: transcriptions of {p:captain-william-somerville|Captain William}'s diary, letters, an entry in {t:crisps-visitation|Crisp's}, portraits, and photographs of Pat's prison camp {q:124, 132, 452}. He also has Bellingham Arthur's office diary and personal diary (transcript B: "I'm fortunate enough to have both his office diary and his personal diary" {q:T2:133}; A hears "Unfortunate enough" {q:334}), and refers to an article about Pat's escape {q:T2:173}.

{ctx}The National Library of Ireland's list of the Rooke Papers (1998) notes that the Somerville Papers, the research of Bellingham Arthur Somerville that his daughter Cecil B. Rooke used, "are now in the possession of Mr. William Somerville" {s:nli-rooke}. {int}This is almost certainly the narrator, who speaks of owning Bellingham Arthur's diaries {q:T2:133}.

A second recording, made the next day (transcript C), is spent over the family's papers. The narrator shows the family Bible, his grandfather's notebooks, the family's annotated copy of the Visitation of Ireland, Lily Somerville's confirmation of arms, a 1929 newspaper cutting, the pedigree rolls of the 1950s and the portraits {q:T3:4-34} {q:T3:76-96} {q:T3:177-188} {q:T3:236-275}. He is writing a profile of every member of the family, "branch" by branch, with his own additions in red {q:T3:150-153} {q:T3:195}, and plans to share them with the family and with a cousin, David Gilmour {q:T3:167-168} {q:T3:194}.

He is also pursuing the claim his father began: "the claim that my father started to make that my father and now I am the present Baronet and that has to be approved" by the College of Arms, "a very lengthy process" {q:T3:71-72}. He and his son Edward visited the College in London in August, "three Augusts ago" {q:T3:70}; the pursuivant dealing with the claim, Phillip Bone, "was optimistic" but wanted to consult a colleague {q:T3:139-140} ({qn:q-baronetcy-succession}). Of the succession after him he says: "If I die, James is the next heir … Then it goes to Charles" {q:T3:73}.

name: Gergely Somerville
summary: The interviewer: the narrator's grandson, son of {p:charles-somerville|Charles Somerville}, who recorded the conversation and had already begun research on Ancestry.
bio: Gergely Somerville, the narrator's grandson and the son of {p:charles-somerville|Charles Somerville}, recorded the conversation (relationships confirmed by the family in 2026). He brought printouts from an online family tree on Ancestry {q:114-120, 518-524} and asks many of the clarifying questions in the transcript.

On his mother's side his family is Hungarian: he speaks of his grandfather Miklós and of a great-grandmother in Eger, whose story of her husband's escape from a gulag is recorded as an open question {q:568} {q:588-598} {q:T2:225} {q:T2:235-240} ({qn:q-hungarian-family}).

He recorded a second conversation the next day, over the family's papers and portraits (transcript C), for an assignment in his college course in cultural and heritage studies {q:T3:282}. He was baptised at St Audoen's Church, Dublin, in 2006, according to the narrator's roll of the family {q:T3:185} {q:T3:6}, the church where Bellingham Arthur's children were baptised {s:visitation-1897}. Marcus, one of his middle names, recalls the portrait of Sir Marcus Somerville: "I remember specifically the portrait of Marcus because it's one of my … middle names" {q:T3:52-53}. In the second recording he contributes his own research: the bayonet at Youghal and the cause of the riot {q:T3:164-165}, the Bâby family of Detroit {q:T3:269}, and a DNA test linking him to a descendant of Vere {q:T3:201}.

summary: Lord Mayor of Dublin (1736–37) and MP for Dublin City, created a baronet in 1748. The narrator calls him simply "the first baronet".
bio: The narrator never names him, describing {p:major-william-somerville|Major William Somerville} as "the second son of the first baronet" {q:84}. The identification with Sir James Somerville is ours: the Somerville baronetcy of 1748 is the one that, as the narrator says, "became dormant" in January 1929 {q:174}, and published accounts independently name a second son, Major William Somerville {s:wp-sir-james-somerville}.

{ctx}Sir James Somerville (c. 1698–1748) sat for Dublin City in the Irish House of Commons from 1729, was Lord Mayor of Dublin in 1736–37, and was created a baronet "of Somerville, County Meath" on 14 February 1748, a few months before his death {s:wp-sir-james-somerville}. His eldest son Quaile succeeded to the title {s:wp-athlumney}.

{ctx}A compiled online genealogy, citing the Stirnet Somerville pedigree, also lists among his children "William Somerville" (1720–1780), "a Major in the Army" {s:winters-p66}, which supports the narrator's account of a second son, Major William {q:84} {q:T2:40-41}. It gives his wife's name as Elizabeth Quaile, daughter of Alderman William Quaile, where Wikipedia has Elizabeth Quayle, daughter of James Quayle {s:winters-p66} {s:wp-sir-james-somerville}.

In the second recording the 1924 confirmation of arms, as the narrator reads it, calls him "Sir James Somerville of the City of Dublin baronet M P" {q:T3:82}; the interviewer adds that he was Lord Mayor {q:T3:16}. The narrator traces "the main branch, the senior branch" from him through Quaile, James Quaile and Marcus {q:T3:52-53}, and shows a miniature of him {q:T3:272}.

summary: Chief Secretary for Ireland 1847–52, later Baron Athlumney. The narrator credits this "cousin" with securing Tenison Alan Somerville's appointment in the Constabulary.
bio: The narrator: "His cousin, Sir William, was head of the RIC among other things. He was Chief Secretary of Ireland … high up in politics and he's clearly secured an appointment for his young cousin" {q:212-214}.

{ctx}William Meredyth Somerville (1802–1873), MP for Drogheda from 1837, was Under-Secretary of State for the Home Department 1846–47 and Chief Secretary for Ireland from 22 July 1847 to 21 February 1852, the worst years of the Great Famine {s:wp-1st-baron}. The Chief Secretary was the government minister responsible for Irish administration, including the police {s:wp-chief-secretary}. He was created Baron Athlumney (1863) and Baron Meredyth (1866) {s:wp-athlumney}.

{int}Strictly he was not "head of the RIC" (the force had its own Inspector-General) but, as Chief Secretary, he was the minister to whom it answered, so the narrator's description is a fair summary. By our reconstruction he and {p:tenison-alan-somerville|Tenison Alan} were second cousins once removed, both descending from {p:james-somerville-1bt|Sir James, 1st Bt}. Note the timing: Tenison returned to Ireland in 1840 {q:204}, but Sir William only became Chief Secretary in 1847, so either the appointment came some years after Tenison's return, or Sir William's influence was exercised before he held that office (see {qn:q-tenison-appointment}).

In the second recording the narrator first confuses him with his son and calls him "a Tory, very right-wing", then corrects himself: "his son was Sir William, I beg your pardon … Marcus' son, William Meredith, was the first Baron of Thumbnail [Athlumney]. And he was a politician. He was a Whig. He wasn't a Tory" {q:T3:57-59}; he was "Chief Secretary during the famine" {q:T3:57}. "He married, they had two marriages", the first to a daughter of Slane Castle, and "he had only one surviving son from the two marriages. And that son was the second Baron" {q:T3:59-60}. The first wife was "a Miss Cunningham [Conyngham] … from Staincastle [Slane Castle]. The daughter of the woman who was King George IV's mistress" {q:T3:129-130}.

{ctx}Wikipedia confirms each point: a Liberal; married first, in 1832, Lady Maria Harriet Conyngham (d. 1843), daughter of the 1st Marquess Conyngham, and secondly, in 1860, Maria Georgiana Elizabeth Jones; the only surviving son was James, of the second marriage {s:wp-1st-baron}. Lady Maria's mother, Elizabeth, Marchioness Conyngham, is "thought to be the last mistress of King George IV" {s:wp-conyngham}. {int}The narrator's story that the almost straight road from Dublin to Slane was built so that the king could visit her {q:T3:128-129} is a well-known local tradition; it is not confirmed by the sources checked.

name: James Somerville, 2nd Baron Athlumney
fullName: James Herbert Gustavus Meredyth Somerville, 2nd Baron Athlumney, 6th Bt

born.note: Baptised at Kentstown, Co. Meath, 25 April 1865.

summary: The last recognised holder of the Somerville baronetcy: soldier, courtier and spendthrift, in the family's account. On his death without children in January 1929 his peerages became extinct, the baronetcy dormant, and the Somerville estate passed under his will to his wife's nephew, Quentin Agnew.
bio: The narrator: "The Somerville baronetcy became dormant when the then Baron died in January 1929. And it has been dormant ever since" {q:174}. He raises this to explain why the legitimacy of {p:little-archie|"little Archie"} matters (see {qn:q-archibald-marriage}).

{ctx}The 2nd Baron Athlumney died on 8 January 1929 at Somerville, Co. Meath, without issue; the baronies became extinct and the baronetcy (created 1748) became dormant {s:wp-2nd-baron} {s:wp-athlumney}. The narrator's "January 1929" is exactly right.

The second recording tells his story in full. The narrator read aloud a newspaper report of his death: "Lord Athlamne [Athlumney] dies at his Irish home … at his home, Somerville, Ballrath [Balrath], County Meath … Lord Athlumney, who owned 10,000 acres in addition to his Irish barony, was also Baron Meredith of the United Kingdom and a baronet. There is no heir to the barony. Major William A.T.B. Somerville is heir to the baronetcy" {q:T3:91-92}. It continues: aged 63, educated at Harrow, he succeeded his father in 1873, married in 1919, was page of honour and ADC to three Viceroys of Ireland, served in the Coldstream Guards and the Egyptian Army and as ADC to Kitchener, in the Dongola expedition of 1896 and in South Africa, and during the Great War was "Provence [Provost] Marshal of London" {q:T3:93-96}. {ctx}Wikipedia agrees on his birth (1865), Harrow, succession (1873), the Coldstream Guards, Dongola and despatches, South Africa and the London provost marshal's office, though not on Kitchener or the Egyptian Army {s:wp-2nd-baron}.

{sensitive}The family's view of him is unflattering: "a spendthrift and a gambler and was interested in the theatre and the girls of the cast" {q:T3:63}; "he kept great style. He had a house in an expensive part of London"; a Freemason with his own lodge; "bankrupted once, if not twice" as guarantor for a friend in the theatre; "the property was all in settlement … but his personal estate was really quite modest" {q:T3:103-106}. His father-in-law, Harry Boan, was believed in the family to have financed him {q:T3:99}. The narrator adds that he has recently learned of an illegitimate son, born shortly before the marriage, "David Robert Choyce … an eye specialist in England", who "really never knew much about it" {q:T3:89-90} {q:T3:106-107}. This is family information, unverified, and is recorded as the narrator gave it.

His will, in the narrator's account, left his estate to any posthumous child and settled it on his heirs male, then heirs female, "and then finally he left it to the sons of his wife's sister", who later had a son, {p:quentin-somerville|Quentin} {q:T3:108-112}. {ctx}Wikipedia confirms that Quentin Agnew took the name Somerville in 1950 "in compliance with the will of his uncle by marriage" {s:wp-agnew-somerville}. His widow, {p:margery-boan|Margery Boan}, held the estate until her death in 1946 {s:wp-2nd-baron}.

{ctx}In fact she had married Peter Agnew in 1928, before Lord Athlumney's death in January 1929; their son Quentin was born on 8 March 1929 {s:wp-peter-agnew} {s:wp-agnew-somerville} (see Incorrect information). Which of the Boan sisters was the elder is not established here.

And Major William Somerville was the second son of the first baronet, and inherited an estate in County Kildare called Ardrass … There was a large house and a lot of land" {q:84-86}. The narrator places this in "the mid 1700s" and notes that the lands, as was usual, were let to tenants {q:86}.

He married first, before 1744, a Sarah, by whom he had three daughters (Ann, who married P. P. Kildare [who was 2nd son of Sir James Somerville, Bart., of Somerville]", and Captain William his only son, by his second wife Elizabeth, daughter of James Munroe {s:visitation-1897}. The 1924 confirmation of arms names him as the common ancestor: Lily Somerville's father Henry "was great-grandson of william somerville major in his majesty's army second son of sir james somerville", as the narrator read it {q:T3:82}, and the arms were confirmed to "the descendants of the Major Somerville in His Majesty's Army" {q:T3:85} {s:nli-arms-1924}. Reading the pedigree, the narrator corrects himself: "It's actually not Major William, however. This is actually Captain William" {q:T3:17}.

summary: Army and militia officer, diarist and father of ten. His nightly diary, partly destroyed, is the source of the family's most detailed early stories.
bio: Son of {p:major-william-somerville|Major William} {q:84}. As a young man he "certainly was a regular officer"; family tradition puts him in the South (or North) Cork Light Infantry, though "searches have been made in the military records" without confirming it {q:54-56}. Later he was an officer of militia, which the narrator compares to the Territorials {q:56-58}. Transcript B is explicit: "Later on, he was in the Louth, that's the County Louth Militia" {q:T2:28-29}; transcript A garbles the same words as "the Laos. That's the country. Love militia" {q:56}. A compiled genealogy also calls him "a captain in the Louth militia" {s:winters-p67}, the regiment of his father-in-law {p:henry-bellingham-ltcol|Henry Bellingham} {s:lf-bellingham}.

He married {p:eliza-bellingham|Eliza Bellingham} in 1800, when he was about 23 {q:60-62}; the published Bellingham genealogy dates the wedding to 30 August 1800 at Roscrea {s:lf-bellingham}. Half his interest in the Ardrass lands went into the marriage settlement, from which Eliza drew an income; there is no record of him living at Ardrass {q:88-90}.

They had ten children, eight boys and two girls, "every single one born at a different place" {q:62, 84, 96}. The family lived at {pl:cumry|Cumry}, near Ballybay in Co. Monaghan, then at a house called "Farm" (probably near Belturbet, Co. Cavan), and finally in Dublin at {pl:bayview|Bayview Avenue / Bayview Crescent} {q:136, 182-184}.

"Captain William kept a detailed diary … He entered it up every evening, except when he was away from home" {q:132}. Its entry for February 1823, as the narrator remembers it, records that while "Eliza and I and Dorothea" (transcript B {q:T2:63}; A has "Eliza. And, And Dorathea" {q:144}) were away in Dublin, his son {p:archibald-james-somerville|Archibald James} left home for Barbados {q:142-150} {q:T2:64-65}, and later entries record the care of {p:little-archie|"little Archie"} {q:154-162}. Parts were destroyed at the end of the nineteenth century, after the deaths of the older generation (we read this as {p:tenison-alan-somerville|Tenison} and {p:eliza-oconnor|Eliza O'Connor}) {q:132-134}. His and Eliza's signatures are reproduced in an entry in {t:crisps-visitation|"Crisp's"} {q:124}.

After Eliza died in 1839 "the family then went into decline": only he and his injured son {p:bellingham-somerville|Bellingham} remained in Ireland. They moved together into lodgings on the north side of the Liffey, where Bellingham died in the autumn of 1844 and Captain William in December 1844 {q:196-200}.

{int}How long the family lived in Monaghan is unclear. Transcript B reads "At the time, Captain William and Eliza were living in County Monaghan for 19 years" {q:T2:51}; transcript A reads "At the time. Captain, William and Eliza. Were living. About 19 years. Archibald James…" {q:110-112}, which could instead refer to Archibald's age (he was "a boy of 19" in 1823 {q:T2:9}). Both readings are kept (see {qn:q-monaghan-years}).

{ctx}A compiled online genealogy (drawing on an Ancestry family tree, Stirnet and a Bellingham genealogy) lists all ten children with dates of birth between 1802 and 1820, matching the narrator's "eight boys and two girls" {s:winters-p67}. These dates are shown on each child's profile as leads, not as verified facts.

In the second recording the narrator showed the family Bible: "It was said that my Captain William [Somerville] entered in all his ten children here … As they were born or baptized. So I think it's quite true, actually" {q:T3:26-27}. He read Captain William's own entry: "William Somerville, only son of William, born on the 7th of March, 1778, married August the 30th, 1800, Eliza Bellingham II[nd] daughter to Colonel Bellingham of Castle Bellingham in the County of Louth" {q:T3:28-29}, and the entries for the children, with their godparents and birthplaces {q:T3:30-32}. An envelope in Cecil B. Rooke's hand holds "one small page of the original family record entered in the family Bible by Captain William Somerville" and a "copy of the entire record of Captain William Somerville made by his son T.A. in 1850" {q:T3:34}.

{ctx}The family's pedigree, printed in the Visitation of Ireland in 1897 from the same records, describes him as "an officer in the army and in the Louth Militia", born on 7 March and baptised at St Thomas', Dublin, on 11 March 1776; admitted to the Freedom of the City of Dublin on 10 January 1842; died on 19 December and buried at St Audoen's on 21 December 1844, leaving a will dated 14 December 1844. It reproduces his signature from a letter of 29 May 1844 and Eliza's from the diary {s:visitation-1897}. It also bears out the narrator's remark that the ten children were "every single one born at a different place" {q:62}: Leixlip, Kilkenny, Dover, Carrick-on-Suir, Athboy, Lucan, Newry, Dundalk, Loughbrickland and Cumry {s:visitation-1897}. The Bible's year, as heard (1778), is probably a slip in the reading or the transcription ({qn:q-family-bible}).

summary: Daughter of Castle Bellingham who married Captain William Somerville in 1800. Through her the Bellingham name, and the Tenison name, entered the Somerville family.
bio: "A Captain William Somerville and a lady called Eliza Bellingham, and that is [how] the name came in" {q:20}. She "was one of three sisters", with two brothers, {p:alan-bellingham-1773|Alan} and {p:henry-tenison-bellingham|Henry}, brought up at {pl:castle-bellingham|Castle Bellingham} {q:26-28}. A letter of hers survives in which she recalls that "her brother Henry was killed on this day, so many years ago" at Badajoz {q:50-52}.

She drew an income from her marriage settlement {q:90}. In February 1823 she and her eldest sister {p:dorothea-bellingham|Dorothea} went to Dublin "in the car, the night freezing and cold"; it was while they were away that her son Archibald left home {q:142-146}. She later corresponded constantly with her daughter {p:eliza-nelson|Eliza Nelson} in America {q:164-166, 172}. She died in 1839 {q:186, 196}.

{ctx}The published Bellingham genealogy names her as Elizabeth (1779–1839), daughter of Lt-Col. Henry Bellingham and Elizabeth Tenison, who married Capt. William Somerville of Ardrass at Roscrea on 30 August 1800 and died on 16 December 1839 {s:lf-bellingham}. Every particular the narrator gives (three sisters, brothers Alan and Henry, Castle Bellingham, Henry's death at Badajoz, death in 1839) agrees with it.
{ctx}A compiled genealogy gives her birth as 5 September 1779 at Thomastown, Co. Louth, the home of her maternal grandfather Richard Tenison {s:winters-p67}.

The second recording adds the family Bible's entry, as the narrator read it: Eliza Bellingham, "II[nd] daughter to Colonel Bellingham of Castle Bellingham in the County of Louth … departed this life in the certain hope of a joyful resurrection through Jesus Christ on the 18th of December 1839 at Bayview Avenue in the City of Dublin" {q:T3:28-29}. {ctx}The 1897 pedigree, printed from the family's records, calls her "Elizabeth, 2nd dau. of Colonel Henry Bellingham of Castle Bellingham", born 5 September 1779, died 16 December and buried at St Audoen's on 19 December 1839, and reproduces her signature from the diary {s:visitation-1897}. Both records make her the second daughter, so her sister Dorothea was the eldest, as the narrator always said.

summary: Second son, who left home suddenly in February 1823 and sailed for Barbados after getting a servant girl "into the family way"; later in Trinidad. Father, it is believed, of "little Archie".
bio: "An elder brother had gone to the West Indies, to the Barbados, in February 1823. He had run away from home because he'd got a girl into the family way. And of course this brought shame on all the family"; he was then about nineteen {q:16-18, 112}.

Captain William's diary for February 1823 records that while Eliza and Dorothea were in Dublin, "our dear son Archibald had left home, spent a few days in Clonmel, and then taken ship on board the George and Thomas for the Barbados" (transcript B {q:T2:64-65}; A garbles Clonmel as "include Mal" {q:146-150}). Letters followed later that year, one from Madeira and one from Barbados; one of them refers to a child named Archibald {q:154-156}. He later moved to Trinidad, where his brothers {p:tenison-alan-somerville|Tenison} and {p:bellingham-somerville|Bellingham} joined him {q:194-196}.

He and his brother {p:corry-somerville|Corry} "were fond of women" and there are records of illegitimate children {q:126-128}. The mother of little Archie is believed to be {p:elizabeth-breakey|Elizabeth Breakey}, a servant girl; "there is no conclusive proof", but the narrator's research, drawing on the diary and his sister {p:eliza-nelson|Eliza Nelson}'s letters, indicates that Archibald married her {q:108-110, 128-130, 162, 168-170}. "There is no record of that marriage, but it is constantly referred to" {q:170} {q:T2:71}. Yet the narrator also says, in both transcripts, that Archibald "made the mistake of marrying that girl, whereas Corrie didn't" {q:130} {q:T2:58}: his belief in the marriage is firm, the documentary proof absent.

{ctx}A compiled online genealogy, quoting an Ancestry family tree, gives his birth as 13 May 1803 (as the narrator said) and a marriage to an Elizabeth Crawford on 30 November 1836; citing the IGI, it records a son, Bellingham Brooke Somerville, born on 29 July 1852 in St Louis, Missouri {s:winters-p67} {s:winters-p68}. None of this has been checked against original records.

{int}If the 1836 marriage is correct, it does not settle the family question. The bride might be a different woman from Elizabeth Brakey, or the same Elizabeth recorded under another surname, or the marriage might be a later regularisation. The narrator says only that "there is no record at that date of the marriage of Archibald" {q:T2:68}, that is, in 1823. The naming of a son Bellingham Brooke is suggestive: Brooke was the family from whom William Henry rented land {q:T2:48}. See {qn:q-archibald-marriage}.

{int}Why it matters: if Archibald James was lawfully married and little Archie was his son, Archie's descendants would stand senior to the narrator's line (descended from the fifth son) in any reckoning of heirs to the Somerville baronetcy, dormant since 1929 {q:174}. The narrator raises the baronetcy immediately after this story, which is how we read his "the reason that this detail is of great interest". See {qn:q-archibald-marriage}.

The second recording takes the story on. "Archibald James lived in Trinidad from … 1823, I think it was, till 1835. He then came back to Ireland. And in 1836, he married, in a church, somebody of his own class, a lady called Elizabeth Crawford. But because of the previous marriage, to a girl called Brachy [Brakey], who was still alive at the time. The second marriage was bigamous" (the narrator {q:T3:133-135}). Of the first marriage "We can find no record … only in family correspondence. There isn't a birth certificate or a marriage certificate" {q:T3:132-133}.

For the narrator this is the crux of the dormant baronetcy: "the descendants of Archibald James' second marriage are therefore illegitimate and can be discounted", although "on a cursory reading, without the knowledge of … the Family Correspondence and Captain William's Diary", his eldest son by the second marriage would appear to be the heir {q:T3:135-136}. These are the "American Somervilles" {q:T3:144}.

{ctx}The 1897 pedigree, sent in by Bellingham Arthur, gives Archibald James's birth at Kilkenny on 13 May 1803 and his death on 7 February 1871, and nothing more: no marriage and no children {s:visitation-1897}. {int}The narrator's argument cuts both ways: if the marriage to Elizabeth Brakey cannot be proved, the 1836 marriage cannot be shown to be bigamous either ({qn:q-archibald-marriage}).

name: Corry (Corrie) Somerville
summary: A son who, like Archibald James, had several illegitimate children; he married Lucinda (née Simmonton), who had worked in the Somerville household.
bio: "Archibald James and Corry were fond of women … they're constantly having illegitimate children. We've got a whole lot of records of Corry's illegitimate children" {q:126-128}. They "were baptised, and the record of the baptism shows that they were illegitimate; there's a marking" {q:178}. "The mothers of Corry's illegitimate children did not become his wife" {q:130}.
"Corry … married somebody called Lucinda" Simmonton, who "also worked in the Somerville household" and had previously been married to someone else {q:178-180}.

{int}The name is spoken, not spelled: transcript A has "Corey", "Courier" and "quarries", transcript B consistently "Corrie" {q:T2:56} {q:T2:74-76}. A compiled genealogy spells it Corry and dates him 1806–1880, dying at Cleveland, Ohio {s:winters-p67}. Corry was a well-known Ulster surname (as in Rockcorry, Co. Monaghan), and the family liked surnames as first names (Tenison, Bellingham, Churchill), so we use Corry with Corrie as an alternative. He comes fourth in the {t:crisps-visitation|Crisp's} list read out by the interviewer {q:126} {q:T2:55-56}.

In the second recording the narrator shows the family tree of "Corrie Salmonella [Corry Somerville] and his descendants", which he calls "the Canadian family" {q:T3:177-178}, and reports his own research: "It wasn't known originally whether Corrie married this lady Lucinda Simonson [Simmonton]. And that is a piece of research that I did. And I found, this was relatively recently, that he did marry Lucinda. And so all his children were legitimate. He only had one son, William Bellingham Somerville. And he died without any children. So the male line of Corrie died with him" {q:T3:178-179}. "Corrie and Lucinda were married in Dublin before they went west to America … to Rochester and New York" {q:T3:180-181}. The question had been raised by "the original Garter King of Arms" when the narrator's father put in a claim to the baronetcy in the 1950s or 1960s {q:T3:180}.

{int}This refines rather than contradicts the first recording, where he spoke of Corry's illegitimate children by women who "did not become his wife" {q:130}: those children were by other women, while his children by Lucinda were born in marriage. A descendant's family keeps in touch, and a descendant's wife has researched the family's history {q:T3:181-183}.

{ctx}The family's 1897 pedigree confirms his birth at Carrick-on-Suir on 19 March 1806 and says he "died in America 20 January 1879", but records no marriage or children {s:visitation-1897} ({qn:q-corry-line}).

summary: The narrator's grandfather and the family's first genealogist: an RIC officer at the centre of the 1887 Youghal riot inquiry, later District Inspector at Wicklow and builder-owner of Clermont.
bio: "Our interest in genealogy really began with my grandfather, whose name was Bellingham Arthur Somerville. He was born in 18… It's the year of the Crimean War, anyway. I think it was 1856. And he died in 1916" (transcript B {q:T2:1-2}; A {q:2}). {ctx}The records give 17 November 1853: he was baptised in Dublin in June 1854, joined the RIC aged 18 in 1872 and was 36 at the 1891 census {s:winters-p68}. The archive therefore uses 1853; the narrator's 1856 is kept as his recollection (the Crimean War began in 1853). "He was alive before the fire in the Four Courts and therefore he had access to records which are no longer available" {q:4} {q:T2:2}; "an avid collector of records about anybody with whom the Somerville family are connected", he filled "about six volumes", following up newspaper notices and writing notes on them {q:6-8} {q:T2:3-4}. "As a boy, he was known as Fighting Atty. Atty being Arthur. And sometimes you see him being written as Arthur Bellingham Somerville. But it is actually Bellingham Arthur Somerville" (transcript B {q:T2:11-12}; A garbles the nickname as "fighting atte" {q:24-26}).

Like his father and his elder brother he served in the RIC {q:12} {q:T2:6}. Early stations were in Cork and Limerick, but "most of his stations were in what is now Northern Ireland, Newtownards, all around there" (B {q:T2:116}; A "uternards" {q:294}). He had "a name for attending riots", the "outrages" of his diary, in the 1880s and 1890s "when the Fenians were at large" {q:290-298} {q:T2:117-118}. {ctx}His eldest child, Cecilia, was born at Newtownards on 9 October 1880, according to a compiled genealogy citing the IGI {s:winters-p68}, which supports a posting there around 1880. {ctx}Records fill out his career: he joined the RIC in 1872, aged 18, and by the census of April 1891, when the family was staying with his Clinch parents-in-law at Witney, he was a "Retired D. I. R. I. Constabulary" {s:winters-p68}. {ctx}The family's Ancestry tree adds that two of his children were born at Queenstown (Cobh), Co. Cork, in 1884 and 1885, and that the younger died there in December 1887; by April 1888 the family was at Seaview House, Wicklow {s:family-tree-2026}. That would place him in east Cork from about 1884 until shortly after Youghal, and date the transfer to Wicklow to the winter of 1887–88.

{sensitive}The narrator prefaced the next story with "This now is not for publication. Well, I'll let you use your own discretion, but be careful" {q:290} {q:T2:115}, adding "Be careful with this … because I think it has had a great effect on the family. I'll explain why in a minute" {q:304} {q:T2:119}. The family has chosen to include it.

The family's account: a riot at Youghal "got out of hand", "no doubt over fishing"; "a detachment of RIC was sent by train from Cork to Youghal under the command of Captain Somerville"; "some rioter called Hanlon or O'Hanlon was [cut] with a sabre and killed"; "Captain Somerville and the man who did it were had up, relieved of their positions, suspended. And the whole thing went as far as Parliament in London". "Captain Somerville, while reinstated in due course, was never officially … acquitted … I think that's correct to say that he was never formally acquitted. … It wasn't him that did [it] … he was in charge" (transcript B {q:T2:123-127}; A {q:312-322}, which garbles the last point as "there is no great formally accredited").

{ctx}What the records establish: Hansard shows disturbances at Youghal in early March 1887, when the house of the local District Inspector, Kerin, was attacked {s:hansard-1887b}; an inquest verdict of wilful murder against "District Inspector Somerville and Constable Ward", both in custody (24 March 1887) {s:hansard-1887}; and, on 10 May 1887, that "Sub-Inspector Summerville and Constable Ward, released on bail", were on leave of absence with pay and would "return to duty on the expiration of their leave, as the Attorney General sees no grounds to advise a prosecution" {s:hansard-1887c}. A local history adds that the dead man was Patrick Hanlon, a 30-year-old fisherman from Ballymacoda, killed on 8 March 1887 by a sword bayonet during protests over the arrest of Fr Daniel Keller (a Plan of Campaign case), and that the Crown entered a nolle prosequi; it describes the two men as "eventually acquitted" {s:ballymacoda-1887}.

{int}Who was "District Inspector Somerville"? The parliamentary record names the officer only by surname, as District Inspector or Sub-Inspector (the rank had been renamed in 1883, which is why both titles appear) {s:hansard-1887} {s:hansard-1887c} {s:ukpga-1883-s12}. The archive identifies him as Bellingham Arthur, on the combined evidence: he was a serving RIC officer of exactly that rank, having joined in 1872 and being a retired District Inspector by 1891 {s:winters-p68}; the officer at Youghal was a "young officer" from outside, not the local District Inspector, Kerin {s:hansard-1887b}; and the family's account, handed down independently of Hansard, matches the records point by point: a detachment from Cork, a dead man named Hanlon, a blade, the officer and the constable "had up", Parliament, and reinstatement without a trial, which is exactly what the Attorney General's decision of May 1887 amounted to. The family also connects the affair with his transfer to Wicklow. The limits: no surviving document we have seen gives the officer's first name, and his service register has not been examined, so the identification rests on circumstantial and family evidence rather than a single naming record. Where the family's account differs from the records, the records are preferred: the weapon was a bayonet, not a sabre, and the dispute was over the Plan of Campaign, not fishing ("no doubt over fishing" was the narrator's own guess). The death of Patrick Hanlon deserves to be remembered in its own right.

With his health poor ("something wrong with his foot or his leg"; asked whether it was gout, "Probably, yes. He certainly had a gout chair"; perhaps "rather like muscular dystrophy") and a cloud over his career, he applied for a transfer and "was transferred to Wicklow … he was then in charge of Wicklow and Arklow. Was that how the Somervilles got to Wicklow? That's how the Somervilles got to Wicklow" {q:324-326} {q:T2:128-129} {q:T2:133-134}. He was a District Inspector and "never made county inspector" {q:328} {q:T2:130}. His office and personal diaries, which the narrator owns, show "far too many absences … on leave for a day or so and … owing to illness" {q:T2:133}. He married {p:margaret-hall-clinch|Margaret Hall Clinch}, co-heiress of Clinch's brewery, whose father sent barrels of beer to the officers' mess with the name Clinch burnt out, because his daughter was "marrying trade" {q:240} {q:328-330} {q:T2:95-96}. {ctx}A compiled genealogy dates the wedding to 27 August 1879 at St Mary's, Witney {s:winters-p68}.

He rented houses around Wicklow, where the younger children were born, then acquired {pl:clermont|Clermont} at Rathnew: Colonel Tottenham, who (it was alleged) "wanted to have neighbours that he approved of", outbid him at auction and then sold it to him at the price he had paid; he "took on the repairs and the extensions" and "built the gardens" {q:572-580} {q:T2:227-231}. {ctx}The National Library's list of the Rooke Papers confirms that he bought Clermont in the mid-1890s from Colonel Charles George Tottenham of Ballycurry {s:nli-rooke}, and the Dictionary of Irish Architects records flanking wings and a bathroom extension built for "B.A. Somerville" in 1894 to designs by Sir Thomas Drew {s:dia-clermont}. A compiled genealogy records that his daughter Dorothy died in March 1895 at "Seaview House, Wicklow" {s:winters-p68}, so the family may not have moved in until the works were finished.

The narrator calls him "very snobbish" and "very Low Church"; he "would have had a fit if he knew that any of his descendants married a Roman Catholic", and "he never sent any of his children to school because schools were smutty places" (B {q:T2:134-136}; A "smarty places" {q:338-344}). He died in 1916 "of the flu that was then going around"; the narrator "always thought" it was the Spanish flu but doubts it, since that came at the end of the war {q:10-12} {q:T2:4-5}. {ctx}The compiled genealogy gives his death as 20 January 1916 at Clermont {s:winters-p68}; the influenza pandemic reached Ireland only in 1918 {s:dcc-flu}.

In the second recording the narrator shows his grandfather's notebooks: "He started this work when he was a boy … As you can see, there's very different handwriting here to further on" {q:T3:8}. They go back "to Sir Galter the Somerville [Gualter de Somerville], a nobleman knight, something, came into England", with "his references to the evidences for what he's writing" {q:T3:4-5}, and they "don't follow chronologically … It's just sort of what he learned" {q:T3:10-11}. {int}His research shows in his children's names: Alan Everard Whichnour and Dorothy Alrewas are named from Wychnor and its neighbour Alrewas, in Staffordshire, the manor that Sir Gualter de Somerville received after the Conquest {s:wp-lord-somerville}.

He also sent the family's pedigree to the Visitation of Ireland: "This is what my grandfather sent in" {q:T3:14}, and the family's copy carries his own and his son Reginald's handwritten additions {q:T3:23-24}. {ctx}It was printed in 1897 as "Somerville of Clermont, co. Wicklow", over his signature. It gives his birth in Dublin on 17 November 1853, his baptism at St Thomas', Dublin, on 16 June 1854, his admission to the Freedom of the City of Dublin on 19 May 1893, and his rank, "an officer in the Royal Irish Constabulary (retired list), late Captain 3rd Battalion King's Liverpool Regiment", with the births and baptisms of all his children, every one baptised at St Audoen's, Dublin {s:visitation-1897}.

{ctx}The Youghal prosecution never came to trial. On 8 September 1887 the Attorney General for Ireland told the Commons that a nolle prosequi had been entered in "the Queen v. Sub-Inspector Somerville and Constable Ward" at the last Cork Assizes {s:hansard-1887-sep8}. The charge was dropped rather than tried: exactly the family's "reinstated, but … never formally acquitted" {q:T2:126-127}. In the second recording, reading the narrator's written profile of his grandfather together, the two speakers give the arrest "by D.I. Kellen of yore [Kerin of Youghal]", the county jail "with Constable Ward", the weapon ("it was a bayonet") and the cause ("a protest over someone's arrest … Daniel Keller … land agitation") {q:T3:163-165}. These match the records, and they correct the narrator's "fishing" and "sabre" of the first recording (see Incorrect information).

The narrator adds that a cousin descended from Vere, David Gilmour, has collected the newspaper reports of the affair and "concluded that Belanger Martha [Bellingham Arthur] was not a very good, strict inspector" {q:T3:166}; the remark is reported second-hand, and its sense is not clear. The narrator never met his grandfather, who "died in 1916 … 21 years before" his own birth {q:T3:166}. A photograph shows the family at Clermont, with Bellingham Arthur "standing in the doorway behind" and Reginald "the smallest boy, the youngest one" {q:T3:270}.

summary: The narrator's grandmother: English co-heiress of Clinch's brewery, whose money sustained Clermont and whose uncertain domicile delayed the settlement of her estate.
bio: Bellingham Arthur "married Margaret Hall Clinch, Clinch's Brewery in Oxford" {q:240}: "a woman of substantial means … the co-owner of the brewery" after her father died {q:328}. Of the family's three children, the son drank and was disinherited, "and the two girls inherited the brewery 50-50"; her sister Rachel was "slightly older, I think" {q:328-330}. "She had money, and Bellingham Arthur did not" {q:330}.

She outlived her husband by 33 years and died in 1949 {q:386}. "My grandmother's affairs were very complex because she was wholly English … she derived all her money from the brewery in England. She lived in Ireland, and there was an argument between the Revenue in Ireland and the Revenue in England as to whether she was domiciled in England or in Ireland" {q:548}. That delay, and three sons' deaths in quick succession, led to the dispute and eventual sale of Clermont (see {e:ev-clermont-dispute}).

{ctx}Clinch & Co. brewed at the Eagle Brewery in Witney, Oxfordshire, until 1963; the company traded as Clinch & Co. from 1892 and was taken over by Courage, Barclay & Simonds in 1962 {s:bhs-clinch} {s:wp-clinch}. "Oxford" in the recording is therefore most likely Oxfordshire.

{ctx}A compiled genealogy gives her dates as 16 July 1859 (Witney) – 5 July 1949 (Clermont), her parents as William Clinch (b. c. 1821) and Rachel Hall Wright (b. c. 1827), and records three of her daughters staying at her father's house in Witney at the 1891 census {s:winters-p68}. {int}The narrator names Margaret's elder sister as Rachel {q:T2:131}; the compiled genealogy names her mother Rachel. Both may be true; the sister has not been found in a record ({qn:q-clinch-rachel}).

{ctx}The family's 1897 pedigree: "Margaret Hall, 2nd dau. of William Clinch of The Elms, Witney, co. Oxford, by Rachel Hall his wife, dau. of John Wright of Curbridge; bapt. at St. Mary's, Witney, 24 August 1859; married there 27 August 1879" {s:visitation-1897}. As the second daughter, she had an elder sister, which supports the narrator's account of a sister who shared the inheritance ({qn:q-clinch-rachel}). In the second recording the narrator shows a portrait of {p:john-williams-clinch|John Williams Clinch}, "who founded the family brewery", her ancestor {q:T3:259}.

bio: "Cecilia Eliza Bellingham: that was my aunt Cecil. She was the eldest person, the eldest child" {q:218}. "She took up her father's interest in genealogy … she was a very good genealogist. She married a solicitor, {p:henry-rock|Henry Rooke} (heard as "Henry Rook"), her father's solicitor and "years older": "Uncle Henry" {q:232-234} {q:T2:94}. He "was not her first love. She finally married in 1912" {q:T2:97-98} {q:246}.

aliases: Lt-Col W. A. T. B. Somerville
summary: Eldest son: a regular soldier who served in India, commanded troops at Archangel in 1919, married Kitty Harrison and gardened in West Cork; he died within months of deciding to take on Clermont.
bio: "William Arthur Tenison Bellingham Somerville. That's my uncle Bunt … He was the eldest boy in the family" {q:218}, born "about 1884" {q:264}. He went to school only briefly and followed a normal army career via {t:sandhurst|Sandhurst} {q:346}. "Bunt was in India. In the First World War he was in the Royal Lancaster Regiment, and at the time of the revolutions in Russia he commanded a troop that was sent to Archangel, in the very north of Russia, to keep it from falling into the hands of the Bolsheviks" {q:362-364}.

{ctx}The record confirms the narrator. A history of the 8th (Special) Battalion, Machine Gun Corps says it was "under the command of Lt. Col. W A T B Somerville DSO" from 12 April 1919, and the battalion landed at Archangel on 26 May 1919 {s:mgc-8bn}. The initials are Bunt's alone. The same history calls him Royal Artillery, but The Times, quoted in a compiled genealogy, describes him as a Lieutenant Colonel of the King's Own {s:winters-p69}, and King's Own sources seen in search results name "Captain W A T Somerville DSO" and Lieutenant W. A. T. B. Somerville as adjutant of the 1st Battalion {s:kingsown-1914}. {int}So the archive concludes that Bunt was the King's Own officer of the narrator's account and the commander at Archangel, and that "Royal Artillery" confuses him with his brother Jim, the gunner. Whether Jim also held the DSO, as one notice says {s:winters-p68}, is unconfirmed.

He "was said to have fallen in love with an Indian Maharani … They did not get married" {q:370} {q:T2:145-146}. He married {p:kitty-harrison|Kathleen "Kitty" Harrison} of Castle Harrison, Co. Cork, and they lived near Bantry, between Bantry and Glengarriff, at a place both transcripts hear as "Green desert", with "wonderful gardens" {q:370-376} {q:554} {q:T2:146-147} {q:T2:219}. Both he and Jim "married money" {q:494} {q:T2:192}. {ctx}A compiled genealogy, citing The Times, records his death on 13 February 1951 at Reendesert Lodge, Bantry, and lists him as a director of Clinch & Co in 1950 {s:winters-p69}. "Green desert" is evidently Reendesert.

Under his parents' wills Clermont "was to go to Uncle Bunt if he wanted it. If he didn't want it, it was to go to Uncle Jim, the second one. If he didn't want it, it was to go to Pat. If he didn't want it, it was to go to [Reggie]" {q:T2:149-150} {q:382}. As executor of his mother's estate he was later accused by Aunt Eddie of making "a mess of administering" it {q:560-562} {q:T2:221-222}. "It was always assumed that he wouldn't want to live there, because he had a lovely place down in West Cork … But no, he wanted to … But he died", a matter of months afterwards, two years after his mother {q:552-556} {q:T2:218-219}. He, like all his brothers, died of cancer {q:394} {q:T2:153}. {int}"And he hadn't any" {q:T2:220} probably means he had no children; the compiled genealogy lists none.

When the 2nd Baron Athlumney died in January 1929, the newspaper report that the narrator read aloud in the second recording ended: "There is no heir to the barony. Major William A.T.B. Somerville is heir to the baronetcy. He, William A.T.B. Somerville, is my father's eldest brother, Bunt" {q:T3:92-93}. {ctx}The 1897 pedigree records his birth at Newtownards on 8 August 1882 and his baptism at St Audoen's on 27 May 1883 {s:visitation-1897}. Bunt had no son, so the claim passed to his youngest brother's line ({qn:q-baronetcy-succession}).

bio: Transcript B: "Vere Demerly. I can't remember her name. It's Bellingham anyway … the name Vere, that's a very… I didn't know how it was pronounced"; "Then the next sister, Vere. Vere married the second son of the owner of Clonmannon", {p:edmund-truell|Edmund Truell}, who chose to live in England {q:T2:89-90} {q:T2:98-101}. Transcript A renders the same passage "there to money" {q:224} and "the next sister there" {q:246}.

{ctx}A compiled genealogy citing The Times records Vere Frances de Merlie Bellingham Somerville (1890–1976) marrying Edmund Gray Stuart Truell on 14 August 1912, and her death on 18 April 1976 at Onslow, Wimborne, Dorset {s:winters-p68}. "Veer Demerly" is evidently "Vere de Merlie". The Dorset death fits the narrator's account that Edmund "inherited an estate in England and lived in Dorset" {q:T2:101}.

In the second recording: "Aunt Veer [Vere] had lots of children. One of them was called Rachel, and she married … a soldier" {q:T3:198}; another was {p:toby-truell|Toby} {q:T3:202}. Her descendants include David Gilmour, who has researched the Youghal affair {q:T3:165-166} {q:T3:197-198}, and a granddaughter with whom the narrator corresponds {q:T3:199}; a DNA test has linked the interviewer to another of her descendants {q:T3:201-202}. The narrator adds that the Truells "were largely brought up in England. They had little connection with Ireland" {q:T3:204}.

bio: "The next girl was Adeline, known as Eddie or Teddy. Because as children, they couldn't say Eddie. They said Teddy. So she continued to be called Tettie by most of the family, but I've never called her anything other than Eddie. And my father called her Eddie" (transcript B {q:T2:90-91}; A {q:226}). Her "proper name" is heard as "Adeline" (A) and "Edelin" (B) {q:T2:101}. She "didn't get married for a very long time" and "was the businesswoman of the family" {q:254-256} {q:T2:101-102}. She married a Royal Engineers officer "years older than Eddie", "reputed by the family to be the dullest man in the British army"; they had no children {q:256-260} {q:T2:102-103}.
"It is believed by my aunt Eddie that she, as a child, remembered destroying these papers", parts of Captain William's diary, after the deaths of the previous generation in the 1890s {q:134}.

After 1949 she wanted the narrator's father to have Clermont {q:558}. She came close to suing Bunt's widow over his administration of their mother's estate, until "peace talks" divided the proceeds {q:560-562}.

{ctx}A compiled genealogy gives her names as Edeline Botelier Marjorie Bellingham Somerville and cites a notice in The Times of 1929 {s:winters-p68}. {int}"Edeline" matches transcript B's "Edelin" better than A's "Adeline". variants: Gotta Hugh Roger Bellinger and somehow
summary: Taken prisoner in October 1914 near Ypres (the narrator remembered the retreat from Mons), he escaped from German captivity, reached London across Holland and was awarded the Military Cross; later a gardener near Oxford.
bio: "And then there was Pat. He was Galter, Hugh, Roger, Bellingham, [Somerville]. Where did Pat come from?" (transcript B {q:T2:91}; transcript A: "Gotta Hugh Roger Bellinger and somehow" {q:228}). "His next brother up, Pat or Paddy, or [Gualter], I always called him. We as a family have always called him Paddy, but he was known as Pat because he was the Irishman in the regiment" {q:T2:142} {q:360}. Like Reginald he never went to school, but he had been to military college before 1914 {q:346} {q:440} {q:T2:137} {q:T2:169}.

{ctx}The London Gazette of 4 February 1913 lists "Gualter Hugh Rodger Bellingham Somerville" under the Royal Warwickshire Regiment {s:gazette-1913}. Transcript A's "Gotta" and B's "Galter" and "Coulter" are therefore his first name, Gualter. (An earlier version of this archive wrongly treated a published record of an escaped officer called Gualter Somerville as a different man.)

He served in the Royal Warwickshire Regiment {q:360} {q:394} {q:T2:143} {q:T2:153}. The narrator: "in the retreat from Mons, Uncle Paddy was captured" {q:442} {q:T2:170}. "He escaped with somebody and they were captured and he was brought back and he did this three times. He escaped three times. And the third time he got out and he found his way across Germany, across Holland and to London. It took him, the article, I can't remember, was it six days and six nights" {q:446} {q:T2:172-173}. At the War Office "they wouldn't believe him for a long time … And he got the MC", but "he had a tic for the rest of his life. Always looking to see if someone was following him" {q:448-450} {q:T2:173-174}. The family has photographs from "several different camps" {q:452} {q:T2:174-175}.

{ctx}Other accounts differ on the details. Search results for TheGenealogist's prisoner-of-war records describe Captain Gualter Somerville, 2nd Battalion, Royal Warwickshire Regiment, MC, held at Ströhen, who made nine escape attempts before reaching the Netherlands {s:genealogist-pow}; a family post on the Great War Forum also says nine {s:gwf-warwicks}. A Wicklow Heritage article, which is itself based on interviews with the narrator, places his capture at Zonnebeke near Ypres in October 1914 and his escape in 1917 {s:clarke-sense-of-duty}. The 2nd Battalion landed at Zeebrugge in October 1914; it was the 1st Battalion that took part in the retreat from Mons {s:wp-royal-warwick}. The IWM's Lives of the First World War gives an MC in 1919 {s:iwm-gualter}. None of these pages could be read directly, and where and when he was captured remains open ({qn:q-pat-capture}).

In character he was "very unlike his brothers … adventurous and go-getting … a great deal of charm", but "very short" and without his brothers' looks {q:442-444} {q:T2:170-172}. After the army "Uncle Paddy went to the village of Adderbury, north of Oxford, and was a gardener for a local doctor … But the poor man, of course, got cancer very soon afterwards and died" {q:462-464} {q:T2:180-181}. He married no money {q:494} {q:T2:192}. {ctx}A compiled genealogy citing The Times records his marriage to Heather Edith Baker at Longparish, Hampshire, on 7 September 1925, his rank as Lieutenant Colonel, MC, and his death at Adderbury on 10 July 1947 {s:winters-p68}. A grandson through his daughter has been in touch with the narrator {q:454-460}.

summary: The narrator's father and the youngest child: unschooled and sheltered, a second lieutenant through Passchendaele, a coffee planter in Kenya, twice married, and caretaker of Clermont in its last Somerville years.
bio: "And then finally it was my father, Reginald Malcolm John … the youngest" {q:228}, "the only one who was born at Clermont" {q:574}. He never went to school and, before the war, "he'd never been outside Clermont really", apart from Clonmannon; "he was a very keen shot and a fisherman" {q:346-350}. "He was very deprived of education … he was the one who'd never had any opportunities" {q:352-354}.

He was 17 when war broke out {q:348}; after training ("in Lincolnshire, I think") he reached the front in 1916, was at Passchendaele, and "remained a second lieutenant for the entire duration of the war" in the Royal Warwickshire Regiment {q:356-358}. He ended the war in Italy, possibly after transferring to the Gunners {q:362}.

Aged about 22, after the war, "the word was, what do we do with Reggie?" He went to Africa with "a company called Gunner's Venture … started by Gunner officers after the First World War who wanted a job", to "help manage coffee plantations up in a place called Nanyuki, which is about 120 miles north of Nairobi"; "I trekked [he trekked] up there, it was 1920, with an ox and cart" {q:496-502} {q:T2:192-195}. "And then eventually his mother bought a farm": a photograph shows him, "virtually a schoolboy", at a thatched hut. "That was the farm. And he built it up" (transcript B {q:T2:196}; transcript A garbles this {q:504}). The farm was "a long way from Nanyuki" according to B {q:T2:197}, "Long way from UK" according to A {q:504} ({qn:q-kenya-farm}). On leave in 1928 he married "a girl from Greystokes [Greystones?] called Maudie Moore. She came from the County Laois family" {q:496} {q:506-508} {q:T2:197}; their daughter {p:juanita|Juanita} was born in Kenya in 1932, and two years later Maudie died on the voyage home, so that "he arrived back in Ireland as a widower" {q:508-510} {q:T2:197-199}.

"There was a European nanny, and it was alleged that she had her claws out for young Reggie … He was 38 at the time" {q:T2:199} {q:510}. Staying at Clermont, he met again "a childhood friend, who was the daughter of the rector of Wicklow … And they got married. And they were my parents": {p:honor-johnson|Honor Johnson} {q:512-514} {q:T2:200-201}. The narrator was born in 1937 {q:516} {q:T2:201}. Under his parents' wills Reggie was fourth in line for Clermont {q:T2:149-150}; after 1949 he looked after the empty house but did not own it, and he and Honor "felt that they could never afford it" {q:380} {q:560} {q:T2:149} {q:T2:221}. He smoked, and died of cancer like all his brothers {q:394} {q:568-570} {q:T2:153} {q:T2:226}.

{ctx}The family's Ancestry tree fills in dates the recording leaves open {s:family-tree-2026}. Reginald's birth was registered in 1897 in Rathdrum district, which includes Clermont. He landed in London from Beira on 5 April 1935 with the infant Juanita, so Maudie's death at sea fell early in 1935, not 1934 as the narrator remembered; "38 at the time" fits that year. He married Honor Johnson in the spring of 1936, the year before the narrator's birth. He died in July 1971 and is buried at Delgany. His full name was Reginald Malcolm John Bellingham Somerville, as a 1940 newspaper index gives it and the narrator's "Reginald Malcolm John" begins it.

In the second recording the narrator reads his father's birth from the family's copy of the Visitation of Ireland, where Reginald had written in his own entry: "That's my father's writing … So, my father was born on the 14th of February, 1897. And then it says, see volume two. Additions" {q:T3:14} {q:T3:24}. {ctx}The printed additions agree: "Reginald Malcolm John Bellingham Somerville, born at Clermont 14 February 1897" {s:visitation-additions}.

It was Reginald who "started to make" the claim that he, and now the narrator, is the baronet {q:T3:71}; pedigree rolls were prepared "in the 1950s … in order to put the claim in" {q:T3:188}, and "the original Garter King of Arms" questioned the legitimacy of Corry's line {q:T3:180}. Like several of the family he had a slight speech impediment: "he couldn't say cloth. C-L-O-T-H. He talked about a rag. To avoid having to say cloth" {q:T3:22}. He "had a great respect for Churchill" and collected his war memoirs {q:T3:37}.

name: Alan Bellingham (c. 1773–1821)
summary: Eliza's elder brother: "unsuccessful" and "unstable", he married the French-Canadian Monique Bâby, could not keep up the estate, and lost Castle Bellingham to his uncle Sir William.
bio: "The oldest of whom was … I think I would use the word unsuccessful. He was a senior member of the Bellingham family … but they could never afford to maintain the estate" {q:28-30}. "As a young man he had been in Canada because there was a cousin who was a regimental officer in Canada and he appears in the records as … giving a leg up to a number of family members" (transcript B {q:T2:15-16}; A garbles "regimental officer" as "regiment law for sale" {q:30-34}). He "married a French Canadian lady called Monique Bâby" {q:30}. "Otherwise … I'm going to use the word unstable … he was completely unable to maintain the estate, and he sold it, actually, to his uncle" {q:36}. He and Monique "went to live in England. Their marriage was not successful"; "Alan fades out. I can't remember what the end of Alan was" {q:40-42}.

{ctx}The published genealogy: Alan (c. 1773–1821) inherited Castle Bellingham from his father in 1800 and "went to Canada"; he married Monique, daughter of Jacques Duperon Bâby, a Montreal fur trader, at Detroit on 22 March 1795; they separated in 1815, after which he moved to London. He rented the estate to his uncle Sir William, and his widow had sold the freehold to Sir William by 1824 {s:lf-bellingham}. The narrator's "he sold it to his uncle" is therefore close to the published account, but the final sale seems to have been made by Monique after his death.

{int}A portrait in the family collection is labelled on the back "Wicked Alan, son of Henry Bellingham" and "probably" {q:T3:273-274}. Two Alans fit that description: this Alan, son of Lt-Col. Henry, the "unsuccessful" heir of the first recording {q:28-30}, and his grandfather {p:alan-bellingham-1709|Alan} (1709–96), son of Henry Bellingham, MP {s:lf-bellingham}. Kingsley calls neither of them wicked; which, if either, earned the name is open ({qn:q-wicked-alan}).

summary: French-Canadian wife of Alan Bellingham, whose portrait hangs in the family drawing room. After the marriage failed she settled at Lyme Regis, the "seaside town in the West Country" of the recording.

Monique [Bâby] settled in the West Country, in Devonland, there's a very interesting booklet about her life, Seaside Town, and I'm trying to remember the name of it now" (transcript B {q:T2:20-21}).

{ctx}The published genealogy: she was the daughter of Jacques Duperon Bâby, fur trader of Montreal; married Alan at Detroit in 1795; separated in 1815 and "settled at Lyme Regis (Dorset)", where she died on 30 July 1856 and was buried at the Catholic church; it cites an article about her published by the Lyme Regis Museum {s:lf-bellingham}. {int}Transcript B makes clear that the booklet is about Monique (A garbles the passage as "Alan. The spelling Bâby comes from the published genealogy; the transcripts give Babe, Babet, Babé and Babel.

{int}The Bâbys were a prominent early French settler family of Detroit and Upper Canada. The narrator's "one of the Bellinghams was a descendant of an early settler in Canada" {q:34} may be a memory of this connection.

Her portrait is in the family collection: "That's Monique Beauvais [Bâby], the French Canadian", says the narrator; the interviewer adds that her family, "B-A-B-Y, I think", were "early settlers of Detroit" {q:T3:269}.

{ctx}Patrick Hanlon, a 30-year-old fisherman from Ballymacoda, died on 8 March 1887 when the RIC charged a crowd in Youghal with fixed bayonets; his death was registered as caused by a "wound inflicted by sword bayonet". The second recording explains. Lord Athlumney's will settled his estates, failing heirs of his own, on "the sons of his wife's sister … there was a son born, and that son was Quentin. And he then became entitled to the Somerville Estates in County Meath" {q:T3:110-112}. "But in fact, he wasn't a Somerville. He wasn't even an illegitimate Somerville. His father was a naval man … his name was Agnew" {q:T3:112-113}; he "had to change his surname from Agnew to Somerville. And he had to bear the arms of Somerville" {q:T3:113}, and inherited after Lady Athlumney's death in 1946 {q:T3:114}. As heir to his father's own baronetcy he became "Sir Quentin Agnew Somerville. Nothing to do with the Somerville baronetcy" {q:T3:116}.

{ctx}Wikipedia confirms the outline: Quentin Charles Agnew (8 March 1929 – 2010), son of Peter Agnew and Enid Boan, took the additional surname Somerville by Royal Licence in 1950, "in compliance with the will of his uncle by marriage", the 2nd Baron Athlumney, and combined the Somerville arms with his own; he succeeded his father as 2nd baronet of the Agnew creation {s:wp-agnew-somerville} {s:wp-peter-agnew}. He came of age in March 1950, which fits the narrator's account of a condition tied to his majority {q:T3:113-114}.

The narrator says he "went to the Isle of Man in about 1970" and sold Somerville, at about the time of the 1975 wealth tax {q:T3:121} {q:T3:124}. His descendants are named in the recording {q:T3:117-118}; as living people they are not profiled here.

summary: Henry Bellingham Somerville's only child and the narrator's father's first cousin. "Interested in family affairs", she obtained the confirmation of the family's arms in 1924.
bio: "My father's first cousin, that is the daughter of his uncle … Henry had one daughter, Elizabeth Mary, known as Lily. She was interested in family affairs. And in the 1930s, I think it was, she … got a confirmation of arms, i.e. the king confirming that the arms which her father and brothers and ancestors had used were authentic and in use from time immemorial" (the narrator {q:T3:77-78}). He holds "the original confirmation of arms that she got", with its seal {q:T3:79} {q:T3:87}.

Reading the document aloud, he gives its terms: an application by "Elizabeth Mary Somerville of 74 [More]hampton Road in the City of Dublin, only child of Henry Bellingham Somerville, District Inspector, Royal Irish Constabulary" {q:T3:81}, who was "great-grandson of william somerville major in his majesty's army second son of sir james somerville of the city of dublin baronet m p" {q:T3:82}; and a confirmation of the arms to "Elizabeth Mary Somerville and the descendants of the Major Somerville in His Majesty's Army" {q:T3:85}.

{ctx}The National Library of Ireland's catalogue of the Genealogical Office register "Grants and Confirmations of Arms", vol. M (1920–29), describes the register copy: a confirmation dated 2 April 1924 to the descendants of Major William Somerville, son of Sir James Somerville, Bart., extended to Elizabeth Mary Somerville of Morehampton Road, Dublin, only child of Henry Bellingham Somerville {s:nli-arms-1924}. The date was therefore 1924, not "the 1930s" (see Incorrect information). Sir Nevile Wilkinson, who signed it, was Ulster King of Arms from 1908 to 1940 {s:wp-ulster-king-of-arms}.

{ctx}She was born in Dublin on 29 March 1881 and baptised at St Stephen's on 5 May {s:visitation-1897}. The arms confirmed in 1924 are those printed with the family's pedigree in 1897, where, unlike the next pedigree in the volume, they are not described as "on record in the Ulster Office" {s:visitation-1897}; the confirmation itself says they "do not appear to have been heretofore recorded in my office" {q:T3:82}.
